key_insight: A compressible finite-chord scattering model can predict leading-edge noise reduction from perforated and porous inserts without fitted acoustic constants by using physically derived admittance inputs.
engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable aeroacoustic design of perforated or porous leading edges for noise reduction in practical subsonic flows, especially where the chord is not acoustically compact.
method: Solved finite-chord, compressible subsonic scattering with arbitrary chordwise admittance
Included wake shedding, Kutta condition, permeability-dependent edge singularities, finite-span and aperture-array effects

Derived perforated-insert admittance from Rayleigh conductivity plus thickness, aperture-interaction, and grazing-flow blockage corrections; modeled porous inserts from permeability and pore-fluid inertia
evidence_signal: Across 84 comparisons for three perforates, the model achieved 2.5 dB rms error versus 4.4 dB with the previously scaled impedance; two porous inserts were predicted within 1.7 dB rms.
watch_item: Measured narrow spectral peaks on perforated plates were not captured by any tested admittance model, suggesting an additional convective source mechanism beyond the frozen-gust assumption.
paper_title: Leading-edge noise reduction by perforated and porous inserts: a compressible finite-chord prediction without fitted constants
